name: Cane River Creole National Historical Park
author: author-B-2026-10-08
summary:
A branch of the New World culture called Creole took root along the Cane River in 18th-century Louisiana, at what the Park Service calls the borderlands between New France and New Spain — a culture nurtured by French and Spanish colonial ways, steeped in Africanisms and enriched by American Indian contact. Cane River Creole National Historical Park preserves two of its plantations, Oakland and Magnolia, 10 and 20 miles south of Natchitoches: in the Park Service’s words the most intact French Creole cotton plantations in the United States, owned and worked by the same families, the Prud’hommes and the LeComte–Hertzogs, since the 18th century. Together they hold 70 historic structures, including eight rare brick slave quarters at Magnolia, and nearly 500,000 museum objects and archives. [n] [n]

Jean Baptiste Lecomte obtained the land grant that grew into Magnolia in 1753; Emmanuel Prud’homme received the grant at the core of Bermuda, later renamed Oakland, in 1789, and after the cotton gin’s invention in 1793 both families turned to cotton; enslaved workers built Prud’homme’s house in 1821. After the United States took possession of Louisiana in 1803, the park’s 2018 brochure explains, Anglo-American settlers poured in with their English language, Protestant religion and their own enslaved workers; life grew more constricted for non-whites as U.S. law removed colonial-era rights such as self-emancipation by purchase. [n]

Congress created the park on November 2, 1994, in the same law that created the 116,000-acre Cane River National Heritage Area — the only time a park unit and a heritage area have been legislated together. The Park Service says the park tells the story of oppressive plantation labor systems founded on slavery and replaced by tenant farming, sharecropping and day labor through the 1970s. [n]

indigenous.html:
Before there was a French post at Natchitoches, this valley was Caddo country. By the end of the 1400s the Caddo numbered about 200,000, and the Red River valley was among the most densely settled parts of their homeland. Then came European disease and a years-long drought: archaeological evidence cited in the 2019 Historic Resource Study suggests the population fell by about 95 percent between 1500 and the 1680s. The Natchitoches confederacy, smallest of three, lived in villages on the river terraces between today’s Oakland Plantation and Natchitoches. [n]

In 1835 the Caddo sold all their lands by a treaty signed near Shreveport, for $30,000 in goods and horses and a promise of $50,000 over five years, pledging never to return to live as a nation within the United States. They went to Texas and later to Oklahoma, where the Caddo Nation is based today. Some stayed or returned, and the tribe still holds the Natchitoches area as its spiritual homeland. [n]

slavery.html:
Slavery built both plantations. Between 1810 and 1860 the Prud’hommes held between 50 and 145 people, placing them in the top nine percent of Louisiana slaveholders. The LeComtes held 234 people in 1860 across Magnolia and their other properties, 112 of them in the Magnolia quarters, completed in 1845. In 1836 an overseer listed the first names of 77 people who had worked seven days a week to bring in that year’s cotton; in April 1830 a Prud’homme cousin sold Phanor Prud’homme a couple, Thibuad and Salinette, and their six children for just over $3,000. The Historic Resource Study cautions that almost everything recorded about these lives was written by planters and overseers. [n]

The brochure describes the cotton year: picking began in August and ran from first light until too dark to see, the hard bolls cut pickers’ hands, and the overseer expected each adult to pick at least 200 pounds a day. [n]

black.html:
After the war a Union commander, on June 5, 1865, told freed people to stay on the premises to which they belonged, and Freedmen’s Bureau contracts at Bermuda paid six to ten dollars a month for men and five to eight for women. Those contracts, the park’s brochure says, differed from slavery mainly in requiring the worker’s consent; sharecropping ranged from a relatively benign feudalism to virtual bondage, the chains of slavery replaced by endless debt at the plantation store. Many stayed and rebuilt a community around church and family, often in the quarters that had housed their enslaved ancestors. [n] [n]

The first sharecropper did not leave Oakland until 1949. At Magnolia the Hertzogs housed day laborers in the brick cabins, which got electricity in the 1940s; mechanical pickers replaced the field crews in the 1960s, and the last residents, the Vercher family, moved out in the early 1970s. [n] [n]
